name: When Trial AI Needs FDA Credibility Evidence
blurb: Which trial uses of AI fall under the FDA framework.
title: When Trial AI Needs FDA Credibility Evidence
answer: AI that produces data the FDA will rely on, for example to select patients, measure outcomes or support dosing, falls under the FDA's draft credibility framework. Purely operational uses such as drafting documents or scheduling sites generally do not, though the sponsor still owns the result.

reading.body:
The FDA's draft credibility framework applies to AI that produces data the agency will rely on, not to operational tools like scheduling or document drafting.

The dividing line is whether an AI output can change a regulatory conclusion. Patient selection, outcome measurement, image analysis, adverse event detection and dose support all shape the evidence a submission rests on, so errors there propagate into the decision. Scheduling visits, translating materials or predicting site enrolment affect how efficiently a trial runs, and ordinary quality controls catch those failures.

For a clinical team the practical consequence is a sorting exercise at planning stage. Classify each tool as decision supporting or operational, build the full credibility file only for the first group, and raise evidentiary uses with the FDA early, ideally before the trial starts. Sponsors still own the result either way, so operational status is not an exemption from responsibility.

The data covers one draft guidance and its scope. It does not say what evidence the FDA will accept for a given context of use, how model risk should be scored, or whether the draft will survive to final form.

explainer:
Not every AI tool in a trial needs the same scrutiny. The useful distinction is between operational and evidentiary uses. Operational uses help run the trial, drafting documents, scheduling visits, translating materials, predicting site enrolment. Errors there cause inefficiency, which ordinary quality processes catch. Evidentiary uses generate or shape data the regulator relies on, selecting patients, assessing an endpoint, analysing images, detecting adverse events or supporting dose choices. Errors there can change the conclusions.

The FDA's draft credibility framework is aimed at evidentiary uses. For each one the sponsor defines the context of use, assesses model risk, and builds evidence proportionate to that risk. Sorting a trial's AI tools into these two groups at the planning stage saves effort, and discussing evidentiary uses with the FDA early avoids surprises at submission.
